overview: CS2101 is the advanced-formation capstone sim for dynamic cruise work and formation contingency support. Be ready to brief pursuit geometry, the stop-training calls, formation abort logic, Section PEL responsibilities, and the section approach contract without turning the event into a tail-chase or local-profile dump.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Cruise maneuvering teaches Wing to maintain position with pursuit geometry and lift-vector placement while Lead provides a smooth, predictable maneuvering platform.

children.text: Lead passes the cruise signal and holds a stable platform until Wing is established.
Wing acknowledges, slides to the 60-degree bearing line, sets the directed power, and calls ready.
Formation references use about 80% torque above 10,000 ft and 70% torque below 10,000 ft before maneuvering; hold the PCL position instead of chasing every torque change.
Cruise position is built around the 60-degree bearing line, safe step-down, and enough range to maneuver without drifting through Lead's 6 o'clock.
Local Capstone source cues the scan as altitude, bearing, then closure: exhaust stack tangent to Lead's wing leading edge, ventral fin over the inboard aileron cutout, and pitot tube on the prop arc.
Lead may use level turns and vertical wingovers; the local supplement frames the work as basic level turns followed by vertical maneuvering.
Lead remains within safe maneuvering limits, including no more than 120 degrees AOB and no less than 1G.
Lead should let Wing stabilize before maneuvering and should start with predictable, wingman-considerate turns.
Wing should keep Lead above the canopy rail during vertical work and avoid using PCL as the primary correction for geometry errors.
Terminate or knock-it-off early if closure, step-down, sun, blind geometry, or energy state becomes unsafe.

items.text: Lead, lag, and pure pursuit describe where Wing points the nose relative to Lead's flight path, which controls closure and nose-to-tail spacing.

children.text: Lead pursuit points ahead of Lead's flight path and decreases nose-to-tail separation.
Pure pursuit points at Lead; line-of-sight movement is minimal, and closure decreases as fuselages align.
Lag pursuit points behind Lead's flight path and maintains or increases separation.
In level turns into Wing, Wing tends to become acute and usually needs lag pursuit, bank, and G to realign.
In turns away from Wing, Wing tends to become sucked and uses lead pursuit to regain the bearing line.
In vertical maneuvering, preserve step-down first; exaggerated pursuit curves can create heading crossing angle, blind geometry, or excessive closure.
Supplement technique: horizontal-stabilizer tip on the fuselage star is pure, stab tip forward of the star is lag, and star forward of the stab is lead.

items.text: Knock-it-off and terminate both stop maneuvering, but they communicate different urgency.

children.text: Knock-it-off is for safety-of-flight issues such as emergency, traffic conflict, blind situation, G-LOC or AGSM failure, area boundary, or any unsafe trend.
Any flight member may call it and should state the reason if able.
After the call, Lead maneuvers predictably, gives directive intentions, and may add altitude and reference heading.
Terminate is an expected or administrative stop: learning objective complete, maneuver complete, or Wing needs to stop the exercise without a safety emergency.
Lead normally initiates terminate, but Wing may request or initiate it.
Lead transitions to a safe attitude, directs follow-on intentions, and clears Wing back to parade or another briefed position when stable.

items.text: An aborted takeoff in formation is a separation problem as much as an aircraft problem. Decide, stay on the assigned side, and communicate when aircraft control permits.

children.text: Brief abort contingencies before takeoff.
If aborting, execute the NATOPS abort procedure, maintain directional control, remain on the assigned runway side, and transmit intentions.
If Lead aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing normally aborts behind Lead while maintaining Wing's side; the interval should provide spacing.
If Wing aborts during an interval takeoff, Wing aborts on Wing's side and transmits once Lead is airborne and Wing is under control.
If either aircraft aborts after section brake release, the aborting aircraft stays on its side and executes the abort.

The non-aborting aircraft recognizes the rapid line-of-sight change, selects maximum power, maintains runway-side discipline, and continues as an individual takeoff unless separation cannot be maintained or it has its own emergency.
Wing must be prepared to avoid Lead if Lead loses directional control, including changing sides or leaving the prepared surface if required to prevent collision.

items.text: A Section PEL gives the emergency aircraft the maneuvering room and authority it needs while preserving mutual support.

children.text: If Lead has the emergency, Lead should make a quick radio call so Wing can get separation.
If Wing has the emergency, Wing requests lead left or right.
Lead transfers lead verbally only after visual contact and separation make the transfer safe.
The new Wing transitions to perch and supports the emergency aircraft.
Wing clears the flight path, provides divert or field information, assists with procedures if requested, and monitors altitude, airspeed, VSI, and configuration.
The emergency aircraft maneuvers and configures for high key; Wing matches configuration if remaining through the profile.
Lead may kiss off Wing at any time.
If Wing remains through the ELP, Wing stays outside Lead's turn and waves off when directed, no lower than 300 ft AGL.
Normally, Wing can safely detach and monitor at high key.

items.text: A section approach is a mutual-support recovery that requires Lead to fly a smooth approach and Wing to maintain visual contact, configuration awareness, and readiness to assume Lead.

children.text: Plan the approach, missed approach, configuration timing, and final separation before starting down the approach.
Weather must be at or above circling minimums, or 1000 ft and 3 SM if circling minimums are not published.
Bring Wing to parade, reduce airspeed, and configure the flight no later than the FAF; earlier may be needed in IMC or VFR on top.
Confirm configuration with a clear visual or radio response.
Lead positions the formation on final and normally flies 120 KIAS with Wing in parade until detached.
Wing mirrors Lead's configuration, maintains visual contact in IMC, and stays ready to assume Lead.
If the section misses approach, execute the published missed approach using normal hand signals or tactical frequency unless otherwise briefed.
If individual approaches are required, Lead coordinates separate squawks and normally sends the lower-fuel aircraft first.
Use current local SOP, IFG, and day-of brief for field-specific detach or landing-flow details.

studyNotes.summary: CS2101 ties advanced cruise maneuvering to formation contingency support: hold the cruise contract, use pursuit geometry, stop maneuvering correctly, and brief abort, Section PEL, and section approach procedures as a connected formation problem.

summary: CS2101 covers cruise maneuvering, pursuit geometry, stop-training calls, formation abort logic, Section PEL, and section approach procedures.
